JSON: Name: hgse2_birefringence_pipeline Title: Synthesis-driven structural design and multi-modal characterization of linear [HgSe]2-containing thiohalide crystals to increase birefringence and extend mid-to-far infrared transmission Short Hypothesis: Crystallographically aligning linear [HgSe]2 multinuclear clusters within a thiohalide crystal lattice causes an increase in optical birefringence (Δn) and a shift of the long-wavelength transmission edge to ≥25 μm relative to otherwise compositionally similar crystals lacking aligned [HgSe]2 clusters. Related Work: Existing strategies to produce large birefringence include introducing planar π-conjugated building blocks, exploiting stereoactive lone-pair cations, and assembling anisotropic layered or chain-like topologies. Heavy-metal multinuclear clusters (notably linear Hg-based clusters) have been reported to enhance polarizability anisotropy beyond conventional units, but prior implementations face trade-offs: materials engineered for high Δn often contain light-atom oxygenated motifs that produce strong phonon absorption in the mid-to-far IR, whereas IR-transparent compounds frequently lack sufficient electronic anisotropy for large Δn. Reported Hg-based cluster materials show enhanced anisotropy but limited transparency windows or insufficient alignment control, and measurement of IR birefringence is often constrained by scarcity of millimeter-scale, optically homogeneous crystals. Computational analyses have quantified polarizability anisotropy of candidate units, but there is a gap integrating targeted synthesis, rigorous small-crystal birefringence measurement, and quantitative attribution of anisotropy to specific multinuclear units. Abstract: We target the simultaneous attainment of large optical birefringence and broad mid-to-far infrared transparency in a single crystalline material by design and characterization of linear Hg multinuclear cluster units. The proposed approach synthesizes a Hg–Ga–Se–Cl thiohalide framework that incorporates well-aligned linear [HgSe]2 clusters and combines structural, spectroscopic, optical, and first-principles analyses to quantify their contribution to anisotropic polarizability. The primary contribution is a validated experimental–computational pipeline that (1) synthesizes and structurally confirms the presence and alignment of [HgSe]2 clusters, (2) measures spectral birefringence on small single crystals using polarization-resolved microscopy across visible to mid-IR wavelengths and temperature, and (3) assigns birefringence contributions to specific structural units via real-space atom-cutting and polarizability calculations. Expected outcomes are a reproducible materials protocol demonstrating a measurable Δn increase and a broadened transmission window attributable to [HgSe]2 alignment, together with transferable measurement and analysis methods applicable to other heavy-element cluster systems for mid-to-far IR photonics. Experiments: Samples and datasets: (1) Synthesize at least 5 independent batches of Hg18Ga8Se8Cl32 single crystals (targeted composition) with typical crystal sizes 0.05–1 mm and prepare ≥10 optically qualified platelet fragments per batch (thickness range 5–50 μm). (2) Prepare control samples: (a) nearest-composition analogues engineered to disrupt [HgSe]2 alignment (same stoichiometry but altered transport/reaction conditions), (b) Hg-based thiohalides with single Hg–Se units (not multinuclear), and (c) benchmark birefringent crystals: TiO2 (rutile), YVO4, and AgGaS2. Baselines: TiO2, YVO4, AgGaS2, and selected Hg-based chalcogenides. Measurement metrics: spectral birefringence Δn(λ) at λ = 546.1 nm, 1064 nm, 1540 nm, 3500 nm; transmission T(λ) and transmission edge λ_cutoff defined where T>50% for 100 μm-equivalent thickness; polarizability anisotropy δ (from Gaussian molecular/cluster calculations); Raman phonon frequencies ω_i(T) and temperature coefficients dω/dT; XPS-derived Hg oxidation-state fractions; laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT) energy density where microcracks first appear. Instrumentation and protocols: single-crystal XRD for structure and alignment quantification; SEM-EDS and ICP-OES for composition verification; UV-Vis-NIR diffuse reflectance for optical gap; FTIR transmission 0.4–25 μm in vacuum for T(λ); polarization-resolved microscope with Berek compensator and calibrated monochromatic sources to measure optical path difference R and compute Δn = R/d on platelet samples (repeat each measurement n≥5 per sample); temperature-dependent Raman 80–423 K with controlled stage; XPS (Al Kα) for valence states; first-principles DFT (PBE, plane-wave) for band structure and dielectric tensor, apply scissor correction; Gaussian-based polarizability tensor calculations for finite-cluster δ values; real-space atom-cutting computational ablation to quantify fraction contribution of [HgSe]2 units to Δn. Experimental comparisons and ablations: (A) Direct comparison: target compound vs control analogues and benchmark crystals for Δn(λ) and λ_cutoff. (B) Composition ablation: synthesize series varying Ga:Cl:Hg ratios to modulate prevalence/alignment of [HgSe]2 clusters and measure Δn and T(λ) across series. (C) Computational ablation: remove or replace [HgSe]2 atoms in periodic supercell and recalculate dielectric tensor to quantify Δn change. Statistical reporting: report mean±SD for Δn and λ_cutoff from ≥5 independent crystals; perform paired statistical tests comparing target vs controls (α=0.05). Risk Factors and Limitations: Toxicity and handling: Hg precursors require specialized glovebox and sealed-tube CVT procedures and regulatory constraints limit scale and reproducibility. Phase stability and hygroscopicity: target crystals degrade measurably under ambient humidity within days, limiting measurement window and long-term device applicability. Crystal size and homogeneity: synthesis may produce insufficiently large or optically homogeneous crystals for conventional mid-IR characterization; polarization microscopy measurements on thin platelets may introduce thickness-dependent artifacts. Measurement uncertainties: accurate Δn determination on sub-mm samples depends on precise thickness measurement, compensator calibration, and control of stress-induced birefringence. Computational limitations: DFT (PBE) underestimates bandgaps and may misestimate dielectric response without GW or hybrid corrections; cluster polarizability calculations depend on choice of truncation and basis set. Generalizability limits: the identified mechanism leverages heavy-element relativistic effects of Hg; substituting lighter elements may not reproduce the same polarizability anisotropy. Laser damage: LIDT thresholds may limit high-intensity applications. Environmental and safety regulations: Hg-containing material commercialization and scale-up face significant legal and environmental constraints.
